item.title: Anti-Environmentalism and the Future of Green Growth
item.content:encoded:
Anastasios Xepapadeas, Athens University of Economics and Business

Simone Marsiglio, University of Pisa

Luca Gori, University of Pisa

In recent years, the global transition toward sustainable and low-carbon economic systems has encountered increasing political and social resistance. This phenomenon—broadly termed "anti-environmentalism"—encompasses a range of behaviors, beliefs, and policy stances that oppose or undermine environmental regulation, renewable energy expansion, and climate mitigation efforts. While green growth remains a central framework for reconciling economic development with ecological preservation, its implementation is increasingly conditioned by public acceptance, political will, and institutional credibility. Understanding how and why opposition to environmental policy arises—and how it interacts with economic incentives and policy design—is therefore a critical problem from both policy and academic perspectives.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Economic, social and political determinants of anti-environmental attitudes and behavior
  • The impact of populism, misinformation, and lobbying on climate and environmental policy outcomes
  • Public perception and resistance to carbon taxation, green industrial policies, and regulation
  • Distributional and equity aspects of green growth as sources of policy backlash
  • The role of institutions and governance in shaping environmental resistance
  • International and comparative analyses of anti-environmental movements and climate cooperation
  • Behavioral and cultural dimensions of environmental skepticism and pro-growth narratives
  • Policy strategies for overcoming anti-environmentalist sentiment and fostering green, just and inclusive transitions
  • Economic growth under increasing climate-related extreme event risk, and the costs of climate skepticism

item.title: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP): trends and reflections
item.content:encoded:
Sanchayan Banerjee, King's College London

Lory Barile, University of Warwick

Traditional environmental economics addresses market failures (e.g., externalities, public goods, asymmetric information), using regulation and price-based instruments under a rational choice benchmark. Decades of evidence on bounded rationality, bounded self-interest, and bounded willpower reveal systematic departures from that benchmark, generating behavioural failures that can blunt or distort policy. These departures are well documented across core domains (e.g., environmental valuation, discounting of future outcomes and assets, and utility maximisation) and have given rise to a vibrant subfield: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP).

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Interactions between market failures and behavioural failures in environmental settings
  • Policy design that combines prices/standards with behavioural tools (defaults, salience/framing, simplification, commitment)
  • Welfare analysis (including psychological costs), ethics, and paternalism in environmental policy
  • Empirical identification of behavioural mechanisms; field/lab/quasi-experimental evidence
  • Heterogeneity, equity, and distributional consequences of behavioural environmental policies
  • Replication, meta-analysis, and open-science practices in this domain
  • Choice architecture and environmental outcomes
  • Interactions between behavioural instruments and prices/regulation
  • Welfare measurement and persistence (including psychological costs)
  • Distributional and equity dimensions
  • Climate cognition and communication
  • Evaluation and methods

item.title: Valuing health and longevity: Advances and innovations
item.content:encoded:
Lisa A. Robinson, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Olof Bystrom, OECD

Ståle Navrud, Norwegian University of Life Sciences

Mortality risk reductions typically dominate the benefits estimates for environmental policies. Recent reviews and syntheses of the value per statistical life (VSL) literature suggest that, while the research base is relatively strong for some settings, it contains significant gaps and inconsistencies. These include the need for more research on how attributes of the population and the risk affect these values. Deciding how to best synthesize and apply the estimates is also challenging.

The value of nonfatal risk reductions receives substantially less attention, although the expected reduction in cases of nonfatal illnesses or injuries associated with environmental policies is frequently large. As is the case for mortality risks, estimates of individual willingness to pay (WTP) are the preferred measure of values. However, due to gaps in the research literature, these risks are often valued using proxies such as averted costs.

Potential topics

  • Value per statistical life (VSL) and population attributes affecting mortality risk valuations

item.title: Wildfires in a Changing Climate: Impacts, Adaptation, and Policy
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Meier, ETH Zurich

Eric Strobl, University of Bern

Robert J. R. Elliott, University of Birmingham

In many regions of the world fire seasons have been lengthening, alongside increases in wildfire frequency and intensity. Climate change, shifts in land use, and the expansion of human settlements into fire-prone areas have transformed wildfires from largely localised hazards into systemic risks with cascading effects across ecosystems and economies. These developments have rendered many existing models, policies, and assumptions increasingly outdated, underscoring the urgent need for robust economic evidence to inform policy and private-sector decision making aligned with current and future wildfire conditions.

Potential topics

  • Labour productivity, sectoral employment shifts, and worker mobility
  • Housing markets, mortgage risk, and migration and other behavioural responses to wildfire risk and exposure
  • Natural capital and ecosystem service valuation, including impacts on biodiversity, recreation, and forest asset pricing
  • Inequality, information access, and distributional impacts of exposure and monitoring technologies
  • Public finance, insurance markets, and the fiscal consequences for local and regional governments
  • Institutions, governance, and risk-sharing arrangements, including coordination across jurisdictions, public-private roles, and firm responses to wildfire risk
  • Prevention, suppression, and adaptation strategies, including land-use planning, prescribed burning, indigenous fire stewardship, and advanced monitoring and management technologies
  • Welfare losses from smoke exposure, including physical and mental health outcomes and associated human capital effects
